title: Touching Materials Visually: About the Dominance of Vision in Building Material Assessment

findings.antecedent: Sensory condition (vision only, touch only, general)
findings.consequent: Assessment of building materials (attributes: complex pattern, glossy, massive, rough, warm, and 11 attributes for interaction)
findings.quote: The Condition main effect was significant for five attributes (complex pattern, glossy, massive, rough, and warm) and the Material × Condition interaction was significant for 11 attributes (all except fragile and denting, see Appendix 1).

findings.consequent: Assessment of building materials (all attributes)
findings.quote: We found no significant differences between the general and visual evaluations of the materials (p > 0.05 for all attributes).

findings.consequent: Assessment of building materials (attributes: complex pattern, glossy, massive, warm)
findings.quote: The tactile assessment (TAC) of complex pattern, glossy, massive, and warm was significantly different (p ≤ 0.05) from the evaluations where participants used vision (both GEN and VIS).

findings.consequent: Perceived massiveness of materials
findings.quote: The materials are generally perceived to be less massive during tactile evaluation than in the other conditions (Figure 1a).

findings.consequent: Perceived complexity of material pattern (wood, blue stone, plasterwork)
findings.quote: the pattern of wood and blue stone is perceived to be far more complex when using vision, whereas the pattern of plasterwork seems more complex when using touch.

findings.consequent: Architecture students' general assessment of building materials (for indoor walls)
findings.quote: our overall conclusion remains that participants' assessment of building materials generally does not change when being allowed to use both vision and touch compared to vision only, which indicates that the architecture students' general assessment of these aspects for indoor walls is dominated by vision.

findings.consequent: Frequency of naming material labels
findings.quote: The test condition related significantly to the number of material labels named by the participants, X²(2) = 97.9, p < 0.001.

findings.consequent: Accuracy of material identification
findings.quote: When participants relied on touch only (TAC), many material labels did not match the material being assessed.

findings.consequent: Frequency of technical and sensory descriptions
findings.quote: The data showed a significant effect of the test condition, X²(2) = 53.8, p < 0.001. Technical and sensory descriptions were used more frequently in the tactile condition (43.9%) than in the other conditions (28.4% for GEN, 22.2% for VIS).

findings.consequent: Association of concrete with 'cold'
findings.quote: Concrete was, for example, most commonly associated with cold during the evaluation in the visual test condition, whereas none of the participants taking the tactile test mentioned coldness in their associations.

findings.consequent: Mention of color properties
findings.quote: And although color cannot be perceived by touch, several participants named color properties in association to the materials they touched blindly.

findings.consequent: Frequency of expressive and associative meanings (personal experiences)
findings.quote: Expressive and associative meanings-mostly relating to participants' personal experiences were mentioned only to a limited extent by the participants in the tactile test condition (34.6%), but came up frequently when they used vision for the assessment (65.7% in the general test condition and 69.3% in the visual test condition).

findings.consequent: Dominant sensory modality for material assessment
findings.quote: The fact that no substantia differences were found between the visual and general assessment for any of the attributes suggests that vision is by far the dominant sensory modality when assessing materials.

findings.consequent: Accuracy of material identification
findings.quote: In the present study, the identification of materials on the basis of touch was in many cases inaccurate, while visual identification was, in the main, accurate.

findings.consequent: Consideration of tactile components (thermal properties, tactile pattern complexity)
findings.quote: the tactile components (e.g., the thermal properties or the complexity of the tactile pattern) appear to be disregarded completely by participants when including vision for the evaluation.

findings.consequent: Dominant sensory modality for object perception
findings.quote: This finding corresponds with the general finding that many objects are perceived first and foremost visually (Schifferstein & Cleiren, 2005; Schifferstein, 2006).

findings.quote: The fact that the number of years of training hardly affected the outcomes of the current experiment might imply that professional architects may have similar perceptual biases as naive consumers.

findings.consequent: Relevance of non-visual senses

findings.quote: the sense of vision dominated the buying process for several products, but that the relevance of the other senses increased during the use stage.

findings.consequent: Attention to other senses
findings.quote: vision seems to capture the majority of people's attention during user-product interactions and, thereby, distracts from the other senses

findings.consequent: Assessment of building materials
findings.quote: The finding that several building materials were assessed differently when excluding vision for the evaluation illustrates the need for a more elaborate consideration of the non-visual senses during design

limitations: The present study was not designed to evaluate the architects' material selection process, but to investigate the perception of materials.
The roles of tactile, auditory, and olfactory perception during materials selection remain to be established.
The study made use of small-scale samples and focused only on the role of vision compared to touch in the assessment of building materials.
Future research using larger samples applied within concrete architectural settings or spaces could provide further insights in the perception of full-scale walls and should include all the senses.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the dominance of vision in architectural students' assessment of building materials, comparing visual, tactile, and multisensory evaluations of six common materials. Findings revealed that while tactile assessment differed significantly from visual assessment for several material attributes (e.g., pattern, gloss, massiveness, warmth), vision consistently dominated the overall evaluation, with multisensory assessments largely mirroring visual-only judgments. Participants struggled to accurately identify materials by touch alone and tended to disregard tactile properties when visual information was available. The study also found that architectural training beyond the first year had little impact on these perceptual biases, suggesting that even experienced architects might share similar visual dominance as naive consumers. Limitations include the use of small-scale samples and a focus primarily on vision versus touch, suggesting a need for future research with full-scale materials and a broader range of sensory modalities.
